title: Withdrawal sequencing and the 4% rule
summary: In what order do you tap taxable, Traditional, and Roth accounts? And how much can you actually withdraw?
detailsHtml:
The classic ordering

Conventional sequencing is taxable first (lowest tax cost on withdrawals, currently in growth phase), then tax-deferred (Traditional 401(k)/IRA), then Roth last (let the tax-free growth continue longest). Modern thinking suggests this is too rigid: a more efficient approach blends withdrawals to manage your tax bracket year-by-year, doing Roth conversions in low-income years to avoid future Required Minimum Distribution shocks at age 73 (rising to 75 in 2033 under SECURE 2.0 §107, which extends the "tax valley" conversion window by two additional years for households turning 65 in 2023 or later).

The 4% rule, refined

Bengen's 1994 research found that a 4% initial withdrawal rate (adjusted for inflation annually) from a 50/50 portfolio sustained a 30-year retirement with ~95% historical success. Subsequent research has refined this:

  • For 40-year horizons, the safe rate drops to ~3.5%.
  • For 50-year horizons (early retirement), ~3.25%.
  • Spending flexibility (cutting 10–15% in down years) lets the safe starting rate rise to 4.5–5%.
  • Bengen himself has subsequently said 4% was meant as the floor — the historical average safe rate is closer to 7%.
Sequence-of-returns risk: The first 5–10 years of retirement disproportionately determine portfolio survival. A bad sequence early (large drawdown while withdrawing) can permanently impair the portfolio in a way the same returns in different order would not. Holding 1–2 years of expenses in cash plus 3–5 years in short bonds (a "bucket strategy") lets you avoid selling equities during downturns.
